title: Colouring arguments
objectives: Prove a tiling or a route impossible by colouring the board.

screens.title: Which square can go
screens.prose: A 5 × 5 board loses one square. Then 12 dominoes must cover the other 24 exactly, each domino on two neighbouring squares.

state.caption: Remove one square, then cover the rest with 12 dominoes.

screens.question: Which squares can you remove? Tap every one.

hints.text: Shade the board like a chessboard. How many squares of each shade?
The corners share a shade. So does the centre.
A domino covers one dark and one light square, so 12 dominoes cover 12 of each.

feedback.correct: All 13 dark squares, and no light one.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Colour the board like a chessboard and count each colour.

byKey.corners: The corners work, but so does every square of their shade.
byKey.centre: The centre works, but so does every square of its shade.

explain.text: A chessboard shading gives 13 dark squares, the corners among them, and 12 light. A domino covers one of each, so the removed square must be dark; search tiles every dark case. Principle: colour so each piece covers the colours in a fixed way, then count.

canvas.caption: 13 dark, 12 light. Remove any dark square.

screens.title: A knight's colours
screens.prose: A knight jumps two squares one way and one square at right angles. Watch the shade of the square it lands on.

state.caption: A knight starts on square A, in one corner. Square B is the opposite corner.

screens.question: Can a knight go from A to B in exactly 7 moves?

options.text: No: every move changes the shade, and A and B share one
Yes: 7 moves is plenty for an 8 × 8 board
options.why: You judged by distance. After an odd number of moves the knight stands on the other shade from A.

options.text: Yes: the board has 7 gaps between A and B
options.why: You counted gaps along a side. A knight moves by colour, not by gaps.

hints.text: Does a knight's move land on the same shade or the other one?
A and B are both dark.
Each move flips the shade, so after 7 moves the knight is on light. B is dark.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track the shade after each move.

byKey.yes: Seven moves would end on a light square, and B is dark.
byKey.seven: Gaps do not matter. Each move flips the shade, so 7 moves end on light.

explain.text: A knight's move changes $i + j$ by 1 or 3, an odd number, so it always changes shade. A and B are both dark, so the number of moves must be even. Principle: a piece that alternates colours meets parity.

screens.title: The fewest jumps
screens.prose: Seven moves are impossible. Now find the fewest.

state.caption: A knight starts on square A, in one corner. Square B is the opposite corner.

screens.question: What is the fewest moves a knight needs from A to B?

hints.text: A move changes $i + j$ by at most 3. How far must $i + j$ rise?
From 2 at A to 16 at B: a rise of 14.
So at least 5 moves, and parity rules out 5.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Bound the moves by $i + j$, then use parity.

byKey.five: Five is odd, so the knight would end on a light square.
byKey.seven: Seven is odd: the last screen ruled it out.
byKey.four: Four moves raise $i + j$ by at most 12, short of 14.

explain.text: Each move raises $i + j$ by at most 3, and it must rise from 2 to 16. So 5 moves at least. Parity rules out 5, and the route shown takes 6.

canvas.caption: A route of 6 moves, landing squares numbered.

screens.title: A tour of the rooms
screens.prose: A 5 × 5 grid of rooms has doors between rooms that share a wall. A tour starts in the corner room S and visits every room exactly once.

state.caption: Start in room S. Visit every room once.

screens.question: Where can the tour end? Tap every room.

hints.text: A step through a door always changes the shade of the room.
Rooms 1, 3, 5, ... of the tour share the shade of S.
The tour has 25 rooms, so room 25 has the shade of S. That leaves 12 dark rooms.

feedback.correct: The 12 dark rooms other than S.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Shade the rooms like a chessboard and follow the tour's shades.

byKey.far: The far corner works, but so does every other dark room.

explain.text: A tour alternates shades, so its 25 rooms run dark, light, dark and end on dark. Each of the 12 dark rooms other than S ends some tour; a search of all 824 tours confirms it. Principle: a route that alternates colours must match the colour counts.

canvas.caption: 13 dark rooms, 12 light. The tour ends on dark.

screens.title: Straight tiles on a 6 × 6 board
screens.prose: Can nine straight 1 × 4 tiles cover a 6 × 6 board? A candidate says yes at once, because $36 = 9 \times 4$. The board is coloured along its diagonals with four colours.

state.caption: Square $(i, j)$ takes colour $(i + j) \bmod 4$, numbered 1 to 4 from the corner.

screens.question: Count each colour, then answer yes or no.

hints.text: A straight tile lies along a row or a column. Which colours does it cover?
Four squares in a line cover four consecutive values of $i + j$: one of each colour.
Nine tiles would cover 9 of each colour. Compare with your counts.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count each colour, then ask what nine tiles would cover.

byKey.r4c1: You trusted the area, $36 = 9 \times 4$. Each tile covers one square of each colour, so nine tiles need 9 of each.
byKey.r1c1: Count colour 2 again: it runs along the diagonals next to colour 1.

explain.text: Each straight tile covers one square of every colour, so nine tiles cover 9, 9, 9 and 9. The board has 9, 10, 9 and 8, so no tiling exists; a search agrees. Principle: area is necessary, never sufficient.

screens.title: Balanced is not enough
screens.prose: Remove two squares from a 1 × 6 strip, then cover the other four with two dominoes. Either choice below leaves two dark and two light squares.

state.caption: A 1 × 6 strip, shaded like a chessboard.

screens.question: Which removal leaves a strip two dominoes can cover?

options.why: Square 1 is left alone at the end, with no neighbour to share a domino.
You took balanced colours as enough. They are only necessary: removing 2 and 5 cuts off squares 1 and 6.
Removing 1 and 4 leaves 2 and 3, and 5 and 6: two dominoes.

hints.text: Draw each case. Are the squares left in neighbouring pairs?
Remove 2 and 5: square 1 has no neighbour left.
Remove 1 and 4: squares 2, 3 and 5, 6 pair up.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Draw both cases and pair up neighbours.

byKey.a: Square 1 has no neighbour left, so it cannot be covered.
byKey.both: Balanced colours are necessary, not sufficient.
byKey.neither: Removing 1 and 4 leaves two neighbouring pairs.

explain.text: Both removals balance the colours, but removing 2 and 5 isolates squares 1 and 6. Removing 1 and 4 leaves 2 and 3, and 5 and 6. Principle: colours can prove a tiling impossible, never possible.

canvas.caption: Remove 1 and 4: dominoes on 2 and 3, and on 5 and 6.

screens.title: Colouring arguments
screens.prose: Each time you chose colours that every piece covers in a fixed way, then counted. $$\#\text{colour } A \ne \#\text{colour } B \implies \text{no tiling}.$$ Equal counts prove nothing, as the strip showed. The cut chessboard in Contest Practice, lesson 8 (Parity and invariants), used this argument.
screens.question: Which colouring suits straight 1 × 3 tiles?

options.text: Colour $(i + j) \bmod 3$: each tile covers one of each
A chessboard: each tile covers one of each
options.why: A straight 1 × 3 covers two of one shade and one of the other.

options.text: Alternate rows: each tile stays in one colour
options.why: A tile standing in a column crosses both colours.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find the colouring a straight tile meets once per colour.

byKey.chess: A 1 × 3 covers two of one shade and one of the other.
byKey.rows: An upright tile crosses rows of both colours.

explain.text: Three squares in a line cover three consecutive values of $i + j$, one of each class modulo 3. Then $k$ tiles cover exactly $k$ squares of each colour. That is the colouring to count.

screens.title: Prove the 6 × 6 case
screens.prose: Put the proof that nine straight 1 × 4 tiles cannot cover a 6 × 6 board in order. One line does not belong.

state.caption: Square $(i, j)$ takes colour $(i + j) \bmod 4$, numbered 1 to 4 from the corner.

screens.question: Order the proof.

lines.text: A straight tile covers four consecutive values of $i + j$: one square of each colour.
So nine tiles cover exactly 9 squares of each colour.
The board has 9, 10, 9 and 8 squares of the four colours.
So nine tiles cannot cover the board.
A chessboard has 18 dark and 18 light squares, so the tiles must fail.
lines.why: The chessboard counts balance, and each 1 × 4 covers 2 and 2, so that shading proves nothing here.

hints.text: Fix the colouring before saying anything about tiles.
What each tile covers comes next, then what nine tiles cover.
Colouring, one tile, nine tiles, the board's counts, the conclusion.

feedback.correct: Colouring, tile, nine tiles, board, conclusion.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. State what one tile covers before nine.

byKey.d1: The chessboard balances 18 and 18, so it cannot rule the tiling out.
byKey.left-out: Every line except the chessboard one belongs.

explain.text: A colouring proof fixes the colours, finds what each piece covers, and compares totals. The chessboard balances here, so it says nothing. Principle: pick the colouring that matches the piece.

screens.title: Drill: T pieces
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes each, as an interview allows. Say the argument aloud before you answer. A T-tetromino covers three squares in a line and one more beside the middle one.

state.caption: One T covers 3 dark and 1 light here.

screens.question: Can nine T-tetrominoes cover a 6 × 6 board?

options.why: You trusted the area. Area is necessary, never sufficient.

options.text: Yes: the board has 18 dark and 18 light, so colours balance
options.why: Balanced totals are not enough: each T covers 3 of one shade and 1 of the other.

hints.text: Shade a chessboard. How many of each shade does one T cover?
Three of one shade and one of the other.
Each T adds +2 or −2 to dark minus light. Can nine such terms add to 0?

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Track dark minus light, tile by tile.

byKey.area: Area allows it, but the colours do not.
byKey.balance: Each T unbalances the shades by 2, and nine odd steps of 2 cannot cancel.

explain.text: On a chessboard each T covers 3 of one shade and 1 of the other: ±2 to dark minus light. Nine terms of ±2 sum to an odd multiple of 2, never 0, yet the board needs 0. A 4 × 4 board does tile with four T pieces, where four terms cancel.

screens.title: Drill: closed tours
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. A closed tour visits every room once and returns to its first room. Compare a 4 × 4 grid of rooms with a 5 × 5 grid.
screens.question: Which grids have a closed tour?

options.why: A closed tour alternates shades and returns, so it needs as many dark rooms as light. 25 rooms cannot split evenly.
The 5 × 5 has 13 dark and 12 light rooms, too uneven for a closed tour.
The 4 × 4 has one: round the outside, then snake back through the middle.

hints.text: A closed tour steps dark, light, dark, light, and comes home.
So it uses as many dark rooms as light ones.
16 rooms split 8 and 8; 25 rooms cannot split evenly.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. A closed tour needs equal numbers of dark and light rooms.

byKey.both: 25 rooms cannot split into equal dark and light halves.
byKey.five: 13 dark and 12 light rooms rule out a closed tour.
byKey.neither: The 4 × 4 has a closed tour; the picture in Why shows one.

explain.text: A closed tour alternates shades and comes home, so it needs equal dark and light counts. The 4 × 4 has 8 and 8, and the route shown works; the 5 × 5 has 13 and 12. Principle: an odd number of cells rules out a closed alternating route.

screens.title: Drill: one square from 7 × 7
screens.prose: Drill, about three minutes. A 7 × 7 board loses one square, and 24 dominoes must cover the rest.
screens.question: In which cases is that possible? Select all that apply.

options.text: A square next to a corner is removed
options.why: That square is light, so 25 dark and 23 light squares remain.

options.text: The third square along an edge is removed

options.why: Area is not enough: removing a light square leaves 25 dark and 23 light.

hints.text: A 7 × 7 chessboard has 25 dark and 24 light squares.
Removing a light square leaves 25 dark and 23 light.
Only a dark square can go. The corner and the third square along an edge are dark, and search finds tilings.

feedback.correct: The corner and the third square along an edge.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Find which removals leave 24 dark and 24 light.

explain.text: The board has 25 dark and 24 light squares, so the removed square must be dark. The corner and the third square along an edge are dark, and a search tiles both. Principle: count first, then build a tiling for the cases the count allows.

screens.title: A mouse in a cube of cheese
screens.prose: Follow-up: the interviewer adds a dimension. A mouse eats a 3 × 3 × 3 cube of cheese one small cube at a time. Each new cube shares a face with the last. It starts at a corner.

state.caption: The three layers of the cube, layer 1 at the top and layer 3 at the bottom. S is the start corner and C the centre. Shaded cubes have an even coordinate sum.

screens.question: Can the mouse eat its last cube at the centre?

options.text: Yes: with 27 cubes, any end is possible
options.why: You assumed every cube can be last. A path alternates colours, so the last cube has the start's colour.

options.text: Yes: the centre touches six cubes, so it is easy to reach last
options.why: Touching many cubes does not help. The colour count decides where the path ends.

hints.text: Colour each small cube by the parity of its coordinate sum.
The corners are even. So are 14 of the 27 cubes; the centre is odd.
A path of 27 cubes alternates colours, so cubes 1, 3, ..., 27 are even. The last cube is even.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Colour the cubes by the parity of $x + y + z$.

byKey.any: Only cubes of the start's colour can be last, and the centre has the other colour.
byKey.touch: The centre is well connected, but it has the minority colour.

explain.text: Colour each cube by the parity of $x + y + z$: 14 even cubes, the corners among them, and 13 odd. A path of 27 alternates, so it starts and ends on even, and the centre is odd. Principle: the same colour count works in any dimension.

ideas: Colour the board so every piece or step covers the colours in a fixed way.
Count each colour: a mismatch with what the pieces cover proves the tiling or route impossible.
Colours never prove a tiling possible: build one, or search.

formula.name: Colouring test
formula.note: For straight $1 \times k$ tiles, colour by $(i + j) \bmod k$.

summary.trap: Area is never enough: nine straight 1 × 4 tiles do not cover 6 × 6, although $36 = 9 \times 4$.

quiz.prose: A 5 × 5 grid of rooms has doors between rooms that share a wall. A tour starts in a corner room and visits every room once.
quiz.question: Can the tour end in the room next to the start?

options.text: Yes, by going round the outside and back
options.why: A tour of 25 rooms ends on the start's shade, and the neighbour has the other shade.

options.text: Only if it ends there after an even number of rooms
options.why: Every tour has 25 rooms, an odd number, so it ends on the start's shade.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. The tour ends on the shade of its start.

byKey.yes: The neighbour is light and the tour must end on dark.
byKey.maybe: The number of rooms is fixed at 25, an odd number.

explain.text: A tour alternates shades, and room 25 has the shade of room 1. The neighbouring room has the other shade. Principle: an odd route ends on its starting colour.

quiz.prose: A mouse eats a 3 × 3 × 3 cube of cheese, one small cube at a time. Now it starts at the centre cube.
quiz.question: Can it eat every cube, each sharing a face with the last?

options.why: A path of 27 needs 14 cubes of its starting colour, and the centre's colour has only 13.

options.text: Yes, by symmetry with the corner start
options.why: Corner and centre have different colours, so the two cases are not symmetric.

feedback.generic: Not quite right. Count the cubes of the centre's colour.

byKey.yes: The path would need 14 cubes of the centre's colour. There are 13.
byKey.sym: The centre is odd and the corners are even, so no symmetry swaps them.

explain.text: Cubes 1, 3, ..., 27 of the path share the start's colour: 14 of them. The centre's colour has 13 cubes, so no path starts there. Principle: count the positions each colour must fill.

quiz.prose: A knight leaves a square and later returns to it.
quiz.question: Can it take exactly 9 moves?

options.text: Yes, by going out four moves and back five
options.why: Every move flips the shade, so after 9 moves the knight is on the other shade.

options.text: Only on a large enough board
options.why: Board size does not matter: each move flips the shade.

feedback.correct: No: the number of moves is even.
feedback.generic: Not quite right. Each move flips the shade.

byKey.yes: Nine flips leave the knight on the other shade.
byKey.big: Each move flips the shade on any board.

explain.text: Each knight move flips the square's shade. After 9 moves the knight stands on the other shade, so it cannot be home. Principle: a return trip for a colour-flipping piece takes an even number of moves.
